scenes.text: Every fall, millions of Americans rake up the best free soil builder their yard will ever produce. They stuff it into plastic bags, drag it to the curb, and pay, one way or another, to have it hauled away.
Then, come spring, they drive to the garden center and buy bags of compost. And a lot of that compost is made from, you guessed it, yard waste. Just like the leaves they threw out.

And here's the part that should bother you a little. According to the EPA, Americans generated about thirty-five million tons of yard trimmings in 2018, and roughly ten million tons of that went straight into landfills.

I'm gonna show you why fall leaves are basically free black gold, six ways we put them to work here at ROOTED, and two mistakes that can turn all that gold into a problem. And stick around for the last method. Almost nobody uses it, and it builds a brand new garden bed for exactly zero dollars.
First, why leaves are so valuable. A big tree's roots spread out way past the drip line, through far more soil than your tomatoes or your lettuce will ever touch.
All year, it pulls up calcium, magnesium and trace minerals, and a good share of that is still sitting in the leaves when they fall. Then every autumn, the tree drops it right at your feet.
In a forest, nobody rakes. The leaves fall, fungi and soil life break them down, and over a couple of years they turn into that dark, crumbly, sweet-smelling layer on the forest floor.
Gardeners call it leaf mold. And honestly, it's about the best thing you can put into your soil.
Now, let me be straight with you. Leaf mold is not high in nitrogen like manure, and it won't replace fertilizer overnight. That's not its job.

Its superpower is structure and water. Good leaf mold soaks up water like a sponge. It's often said to hold several times its own weight. Mix it into sandy soil, and your beds stop drying out by noon. Mix it into heavy clay, and it opens the clay up so roots can finally breathe.
It also feeds earthworms and the fungi your plants depend on. And healthy soil life is what turns any fertilizer you do use into something your plants can actually take up.
So let's not be part of that number. Here are six ways to put those leaves to work.

scenes.chapter: Method 1: Mow them into the lawn
scenes.text: Method number one. Mow them right into your lawn. It's the easiest one on this list. You're mowing anyway.
Instead of raking, run your mower over the leaves two or three times, until the pieces are about the size of a dime. They settle down between the grass blades and disappear within a few weeks.

Turf researchers at Michigan State University have studied this since the early nineties. Mowing leaves into the lawn didn't hurt the grass, and in their maple-leaf plots, dandelions actually went down. They're still not totally sure why.
There's just one rule. If you can't see the grass through the leaves after you mow, there are too many. Rake up the extra and use it for one of the next methods.
Method number two. The leaf mold cage. This is how you make real black gold.

Grab a piece of chicken wire or hardware cloth, about ten to twelve feet long, and bend it into a circle three or four feet across. Tie the ends together. That's your bin. Total cost, a few dollars, or nothing at all if you've got old fencing lying around.
Fill it with leaves. And here's the step most people skip. Water them as you go. You want them damp, like a wrung-out sponge. Dry leaves will just sit there for years.
If you can, run them over with the mower first. Shredded leaves break down much faster than whole ones.

Quick tip. Not all leaves rot at the same speed. Thin, soft leaves like maple, ash, cherry and birch break down fastest. Oak, beech and magnolia are tough and leathery, so they take a lot longer. Mix them, shred the tough ones, and your pile finishes faster.
Then walk away. In about a year, the middle of the pile will be dark and crumbly. Give it two years, and you'll have leaf mold so fine you can use it in your seed starting mix.

So how do you know it's ready? Grab a handful. Finished leaf mold is dark brown, crumbly, and smells like a walk in the woods. If you can still make out whole leaves, give it more time. Half-done stuff is still great as mulch, so nothing's wasted.
To use it, mix an inch or two into your beds before planting, spread it as mulch around your plants, or sift the finest stuff for seed starting. Your garden won't care how pretty it is.
Method number three is the bag method. It's perfect if you're short on space.
Fill a heavy black garbage bag with shredded, damp leaves. Poke a dozen holes in it with a screwdriver for air, tie it shut, and tuck it behind the shed.

Every few months, give it a shake and check the moisture. Shredded and kept damp, a lot of bags are ready by next fall. Some take a second year. Either way, you'll open it to a sack of leaf mold that would cost you real money at the store.
Method number four. Mulch your beds. Spread two to three inches of shredded leaves over your vegetable beds, and around your perennials, shrubs and garlic.
That blanket insulates the soil over winter, keeps the weeds down in spring, and by summer, the worms will have pulled a lot of it right into the ground for you.
Just keep the leaves a few inches back from tree trunks and plant stems, so moisture doesn't sit against the bark. Oh, and hang on for number six. It's my favorite.

Method number five. Save some for your compost pile. Most compost piles have the opposite problem in summer. Too many kitchen scraps and grass clippings, not enough brown material, and they turn into a smelly, soggy mess.
So fill a few bags with dry leaves now and stash them. Next summer, every time you add a bucket of greens, add two or three buckets of leaves. That's roughly the balance a healthy compost pile wants.
And method number six, the one I promised. Build a brand new garden bed right now, on top of your lawn, for zero dollars.
Pick your spot. Lay down plain brown cardboard, with the tape and labels pulled off, and overlap the edges so no grass can sneak through. Then soak it with the hose.

Pile shredded leaves on top, eight to twelve inches deep. Mix in anything green you've got. The last grass clippings, coffee grounds from a local coffee shop, some kitchen scraps. The greens add nitrogen, and that helps the leaves break down faster.
Top it with a thin layer of compost or soil if you have it, water it, and leave it alone for the winter.

Under that blanket, the grass dies off, the cardboard softens, and the worms move in. By spring, it'll have settled way down. Pull back the top layer, tuck your transplants into a scoop of compost or soil, and plant. Tough runners like Bermuda grass may poke through, so keep an eye on the edges.
A lot of folks skip soaking the cardboard, and come spring it's still stiff as a pizza box. So soak it good.
Now, the two mistakes I warned you about.

Mistake number one. Piling up thick layers of whole leaves. Big leaves like maple can mat together into a wet, airless sheet that sheds water and smothers whatever is underneath. Shred them, or at least mix them up with other material.

Mistake number two. Putting fresh black walnut leaves where they don't belong. They contain juglone, a compound that can stunt tomatoes and other sensitive plants. Don't mulch with them. Compost them in a hot, moist pile, and give it about six months before it goes near your veggies.

And one thing you can stop worrying about. A lot of people think oak leaves will make their soil too acidic. In practice, once they break down, the effect on soil pH is small. Oak leaves are great. Use them.
So here's the plan. Mow some in. Cage some for leaf mold. Mulch your beds. Bag a few for next summer. And if you've got the energy, start a new bed for free.
Your trees spent all summer gathering that stuff for you. The least we can do is not put it on the curb.

Tell me in the comments what you do with your leaves, and what kind of trees you've got. I really do read them. And if you want more forgotten, zero-cost ways to build living soil, subscribe to ROOTED. Happy gardening.

meta.description:
Every fall, millions of bags of leaves end up at the curb, and every spring we buy compost. Here are 6 simple, zero-cost ways to turn your fall leaves into leaf mold, mulch and living soil, plus 2 mistakes to avoid (and one myth about oak leaves you can stop worrying about).

In this video:
- Why leaves are such a good soil builder (and what they can't do)
- Mowing leaves into the lawn: what Michigan State University found
- The leaf mold cage and the bag method
- Mulching beds and balancing your compost pile
- Building a brand new garden bed for $0 with cardboard and leaves
- Black walnut leaves, matted leaves and the oak leaf pH myth

What do you do with your leaves, and what trees do you have? Tell us in the comments.
